rv.q: Diamond has something special here and her Broadway debut is a refreshing chance to scrutinize an elite slice of America one rarely sees on stage.
Ms. Diamond's perspective on black life in 21st-century America is arrestingly fresh, and I long to know what she'll try next.

And yet this overstuffed but lively comedy-drama, which opened on Thursday night at the Cort Theater, also signifies a departure for Broadway in its depiction of generational conflict and sexual sparks among a well-to-do contemporary African-American family and friends.

Too often, though, Taylor, Kimber, and the LeVay men (the play's thinnest characters) seem to be floating in a fine mist of wit and writerly flash, while the play itself lapses into the old tricks of cheap melodrama.
Under Kenny Leon’s sluggish direction, the women win the contest, at least in the acting department.
Lydia R. Diamond's rich but diffuse drama about a black family on Martha's Vineyard
That’s what the playwright does to her characters in “Stick Fly.”
But at heart this is a sitcom-soap hybrid that often serves to show how wealthy dysfunctional African American families can be every bit as tiresome and self-involved as their white counterparts.
Marin Ireland and Peter Kim are the hapless couple who seem way too smart for this flat-footed silliness.
The well-acted play, directed by Kenny Leon (Fences), is more like a TV soap opera, with predictable outcomes.
Admittedly, there are portions of the script that seem overly contrived, or a trifle melodramatic.
If not for the superb actors and Leon's fiercely committed treatment of them, the gorgeously messy plot could not keep the play from being a snoozer.
Whatever its shortcomings, it's an exuberant work that will likely prove an audience pleaser.
But too often it settles for raised voices and shocking twists  and the gasps and clucks that they'll elicit from the audience.
But while it makes for great soap opera, it turns out to be mediocre theatre.

cn.t: Diamond's melodramatic family drama about affluent African-Americans explores a rarely-seen milieu with soapy entertainment value, but critics find the plotting scattershot and overstuffed with secrets despite strong performances.

vs.sum: A beautifully restored theater with a stunning Tiffany-inspired interior. The 2021 renovation transformed restroom facilities from among Broadway's worst to a model for the industry, with modern bathrooms on every public level.

acc.note: Elevator to Mezzanine, Balcony, and lower level restrooms. 7 wheelchair spaces across all levels.
